name: Okhrey
tagline: Sherpa homestays on the road to Barsey's rhododendrons
meta_description: Okhrey guide: Sherpa homestays, the village monastery, the Hilley–Barsey rhododendron walk, shared jeeps via Jorethang and Sombaria, costs and tips.
summary: Okhrey is a Sherpa village at about 2,200 m in the far south-west of Sikkim, about 10 km above Sombaria. It is the homestay base for the Hilley–Barsey rhododendron walk, 30 minutes up the road. Come for family homestays, Sherpa food, a village monastery and spring flowers. One or two nights, March to May or October to December.
intro: Okhrey is a hill village at about 2,200 m on the road from Sombaria up to Hilley, in the far south-western corner of Sikkim. Many of its families are Sherpa, and their houses, prayer flags and village monastery set the tone. It is not a sightseeing town. People come here for one reason above all: it is the closest place with proper beds and hot meals to Hilley, the start of the walk into Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary.

That makes Okhrey busiest from March to May, when the rhododendron forests above flower in reds, pinks and whites. Walkers sleep in Okhrey, drive about 30 minutes to Hilley at dawn, walk 4 km to Barsey and back, and return for a hot lunch or a second night. In October to December the village is quiet, the air is clear and the snow peaks to the north often show from the ridges above.

Okhrey is about 130 km from Siliguri, 5–6 hours via Jorethang and Sombaria, so it pairs well with Darjeeling, Rinchenpong or Pelling. For a budget trip it is close to ideal: shared jeeps, full-board homestays and free walks. Book ahead in April, when rooms in the few homestays fill with weekend walkers from Siliguri and Kolkata. Bring warm layers, because nights are cold even in spring. Carry cash too, as there is no ATM in the village.

story.title: Sherpa homes on the road to the rhododendrons
paras: The word Sherpa comes from the Sherpa language: shar means east and pa means people, a reference to their roots in eastern Tibet. Over centuries Sherpa families settled in the Solukhumbu area of Nepal, and many later moved east into Darjeeling and Sikkim. The most famous of them, Tenzing Norgay, made Darjeeling his home and reached the summit of Everest with Edmund Hillary in 1953. Okhrey is one of the Sikkim villages where Sherpa families farm the hillsides today.

For most of its life Okhrey was a farming village on a quiet road. Then walkers began coming through on their way to Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary, and the nearest beds were here. Sherpa families opened their homes, set aside rooms and started cooking for guests. Today the village works as a homestay base in the rhododendron season, and a stay usually means a room in a family house, dinner in the kitchen and advice on the trail from your hosts.

Expect a Buddhist home: prayer flags outside, an altar room inside, perhaps butter lamps in the evening. Food is hearty mountain cooking such as thukpa noodle soup, momos, rice and dal, and salty butter tea if you ask for it. We have not found a written history of Okhrey's homestays with names or dates, so we tell it as it looks today. Ask your hosts how their family came here; that story is better heard than read.

did_you_know: The name Sherpa comes from the Sherpa words shar (east) and pa (people).
Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa who lived in Darjeeling, reached the summit of Everest with Edmund Hillary on 29 May 1953.
Barsey (Varsey) Rhododendron Sanctuary, reached via Hilley above Okhrey, covers about 104 km² on the Singalila Range.
facts: Sherpa homestays, base for Hilley–Barsey walk

highlights.title: Sherpa family homestays
highlights.text: Stay with a Sherpa family in a simple room, eat in the kitchen by the stove and get trail advice from people who walk it often. Full board usually costs about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day, indicative, 2026. Book ahead for April weekends.

highlights.title: Gateway to Barsey
highlights.text: Hilley, the road head for Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary, is about 30 minutes up the road. From there it is a 4 km walk, 1.5–2 hours, to the Guras Kunj hut on the ridge. Okhrey lets you start at dawn without a long drive.

highlights.title: The village monastery
highlights.text: Okhrey's small monastery sits among prayer flags above the houses. It is a quiet place to visit in the early morning or evening, free to enter. Walk clockwise, remove your shoes and ask before taking photos inside.

highlights.title: Rhododendron season
highlights.text: From March to May the forests between Okhrey, Hilley and Barsey flower in red, pink and white. Peak bloom near the ridge at about 3,000 m is usually mid-March to April, depending on the year's weather. Rooms and jeeps are busiest then.

highlights.title: Farm lanes and terraces
highlights.text: Walk out of the village on farm tracks past terraced fields, cattle sheds and chortens. It is an easy hour or two with no fee and few other tourists. Go in the late afternoon, when farmers bring animals home and the light turns warm.

highlights.title: A cheap, quiet base
highlights.text: With shared jeeps via Jorethang, homestay meals included and free walks, Okhrey is one of the cheapest bases in West Sikkim. Outside April weekends you may be the only guests, which means more time with your hosts.

how_to_reach.text: From Siliguri or Darjeeling, take a shared jeep to Jorethang (from Darjeeling ₹150–200 a seat). From Jorethang, jeeps run to Sombaria and some on to Okhrey, about ₹150–250 a seat, indicative, 2026. Most leave before about 1 pm, so start early. Your homestay can often arrange a pickup from Sombaria, about 10 km below. Check current status before you travel.

A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹5,500–7,500 one way for the 130 km, 5–6 hour drive via Melli, Jorethang and Sombaria, indicative, 2026. From Jorethang it is about 2 hours. For the Barsey walk, hire a local car to Hilley and back, roughly ₹1,200–2,000 with waiting time.

New Jalpaiguri (NJP) station and Bagdogra Airport (IXB), both in Siliguri, are the nearest railhead and airport, 5–6 hours away by road. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available online or at the Melli checkpost on this road; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Okhrey has a small cluster of family homestays and lodges, most run by Sherpa families. Sherpa Lodge is a family-run homestay-lodge and a long-standing base for walkers heading to Barsey. Kyilkhor Inn and Royal Barsey Homestay are other names you will see in the village. Rooms are simple, warm quilts are given, and hot water may come by bucket. Most stays include breakfast and dinner, often lunch too, for about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day, indicative, 2026. In April, book a week or more ahead, especially for Friday and Saturday nights.
costs: ₹50–100 per person, more for foreigners and cameras, indicative, 2026
budget_tip: Share the Okhrey–Hilley car with other homestay guests at breakfast; split four ways, the return trip costs a few hundred rupees each.
tips: Book homestays at least a week ahead for April weekends, the peak of rhododendron season.
Leave for Hilley by 6 am for clear views and a quiet trail.
Pack thermals and a warm jacket; nights at about 2,200 m are cold even in spring.
Carry cash from Jorethang or Siliguri, as there are no ATMs in the village.
Skip June to September, when rain, leeches and landslides make the Sombaria road slow; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Sherpa homestay evening and dinner
experiences.summary: Spend the evening in a Sherpa family kitchen in Okhrey: thukpa or momos, rice and dal, butter tea by the stove, and the next day's trail plan from people who know it. It is the heart of a stay here and comes with your room.
body: Most homestays in Okhrey are Sherpa family homes, and the kitchen is where life happens. The stove keeps the room warm, the kettle is always on, and guests are welcome to sit and talk while dinner cooks. It is the best part of a stay, and it costs nothing extra. Arrive before dark, take a hot drink, and let your hosts set the pace of the evening. Children usually join in, and so do the family's dogs.

Dinner is filling mountain food. Expect rice, dal, seasonal greens and a pickle, often with chicken or eggs. Many Sherpa kitchens make thukpa, a noodle soup, and momos, steamed dumplings, and some will serve salty butter tea if you ask. Ask about local cheese such as chhurpi, too. Tell your hosts when you book if you are vegetarian, so they can plan ahead. Portions are generous and second helpings are normal.

Use the evening to plan the walk. Your hosts will know whether the rhododendrons are out, what the trail was like that week and what time the car to Hilley should leave. Most homes go quiet by 9 pm. Settle your bill the night before if you plan a dawn start, carry small notes, and leave the room tidy for the next guests. A thank-you in the morning, tashi delek, goes a long way.

faqs.q: What food is served at Okhrey homestays
faqs.a: Expect home-style food: rice, dal, seasonal greens, pickles and chicken or eggs, with thukpa noodle soup or momos on many evenings. Breakfast is usually bread, eggs, puri or noodles with tea. Vegetarian meals are easy if you ask ahead. Packed food for the Barsey walk can often be arranged.

faqs.q: How much does a homestay in Okhrey cost
faqs.a: Most Okhrey homestays charge about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day with meals, indicative, 2026. Rates rise on April weekends and drop in quieter months. Check exactly which meals are included, whether hot water is by geyser or bucket, and whether they arrange the car to Hilley.

faqs.q: Are Okhrey homestays good for families with children
faqs.a: Yes. Homestays are warm, food is simple and hosts are used to families. Rooms can be basic, nights cold and bathrooms shared in some homes, so ask when booking. Bring warm clothes, a torch and snacks children like, as village shops stock little.

experiences.title: Okhrey village monastery at dusk
experiences.summary: Walk up through the village to Okhrey's small monastery, set among prayer flags above the houses. Visit at dusk or early morning, turn the prayer wheels clockwise and sit quietly for a few minutes. It is free and takes under an hour.
body: Okhrey's monastery is a small village gompa, the spiritual centre for the Sherpa families who live around it. It is not a grand or famous site, and that is its charm. You walk up through the lanes, past houses with prayer flags on tall poles, to a quiet courtyard with prayer wheels and a view over the hills. On most days you will share it with a few villagers and a dog or two.

Visit at dusk, when butter lamps may be lit, or early in the morning before your walk to Barsey. If the door is shut, ask in the village; someone usually has the key or knows when the caretaker lama is in. Remove your shoes before entering, walk clockwise around the prayer wheels and chortens, and do not point your feet at the altar. Small children should be kept close and quiet.

Ask before taking photos inside, and keep your voice low. A small offering for butter lamps, ₹20–100, is welcome but never required. If there is a puja or festival while you are there, stand at the back and watch quietly. Your hosts can tell you which days are special in the Tibetan calendar, and whether visitors are welcome to join the prayers. Never touch or move ritual objects on the altar.

faqs.q: Is there a monastery in Okhrey
faqs.a: Yes, Okhrey has a small village monastery serving its Sherpa Buddhist community. It sits among prayer flags above the houses, a short uphill walk from most homestays. It is a quiet, local place rather than a big tourist site, best visited in the early morning or at dusk.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Okhrey monastery
faqs.a: No entry fee that we know of. A small offering of ₹20–100 for butter lamps is welcome but not compulsory. If the doors are locked, ask in the village for the caretaker. Dress modestly, remove shoes before entering and ask before taking photos.

faqs.q: What should I wear to visit the monastery
faqs.a: Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees, and shoes you can slip off easily at the door. In spring and winter you will want a warm jacket and socks, because monastery floors are cold. Hats come off inside, and sunglasses should be removed too.

experiences.title: Day walk from Okhrey to Barsey via Hilley
experiences.best_time: Dawn start, mid-Mar–Apr for flowers, Oct–Dec for views
experiences.summary: Drive 30 minutes from Okhrey to Hilley at dawn, walk 4 km on a gentle forest trail to Barsey and the Guras Kunj hut, take in the rhododendrons and the snow peaks, and be back at your homestay for a late lunch.
body: This is the reason most people stay in Okhrey. Leave your homestay by about 6 am in a hired local car and drive roughly 30 minutes up to Hilley, the road head and main entry point for Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary. Pay the sanctuary entry at the checkpost, usually ₹50–100 per person for Indians, more for foreigners and cameras, indicative, 2026. Check current status before you travel. Share the car with other guests to cut the cost.

From Hilley a wide, well-used trail runs about 4 km through forest to Barsey, taking 1.5–2 hours at an easy pace. The climb is gentle, so most fit families and seniors who walk slowly can manage it. From mid-March to April the rhododendrons are usually at their best, in red, pink and white. In October to December the forest is quieter and the views are clearer. Wear shoes with grip, as the trail can be muddy.

At Barsey, the Guras Kunj trekkers' hut stands on the ridge, with views towards Kangchenjunga, Kabru and Pandim on clear mornings. Rest, have tea if it is served, and walk back the same way. You can be in Okhrey for a late lunch. Carry water, snacks, a rain jacket and a warm layer, and take all your rubbish back with you. If the weather turns, head back early; the trail is easy to follow down.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Hilley to Barsey
faqs.a: The walk from Hilley to Barsey is about 4 km one way and takes 1.5–2 hours at an easy pace, with a gentle climb on a clear forest trail. The return is a little faster. From Okhrey, add about 30 minutes by car each way to reach Hilley.

faqs.q: Can I do Barsey as a day trip from Okhrey
faqs.a: Yes. Leave Okhrey by about 6 am, drive 30 minutes to Hilley, walk 4 km to Barsey, spend an hour on the ridge and walk back. You will be at your homestay by early afternoon. Staying overnight at Guras Kunj instead gives you a sunrise view.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom at Barsey
faqs.a: Rhododendrons at Barsey flower from March to May. The usual peak near the ridge at about 3,000 m is mid-March to April, but a cold or dry winter can shift it by a couple of weeks. Ask your Okhrey homestay about the bloom before you set out.

experiences.title: Okhrey village and farm lanes walk
experiences.summary: A slow afternoon walk around Okhrey on farm tracks, past terraced fields, chortens, cattle sheds and prayer flags. It is free, needs no guide, and shows the farming village behind the homestay signs. Go when animals come home and the light softens.
body: Okhrey is a farming village first and a homestay base second. Spend an afternoon walking its lanes and tracks, and you see how families here live. Terraced fields climb the slopes, and what grows on them depends on the season: maize, potatoes, vegetables and fodder. Cattle sheds sit beside the houses, and chortens and prayer flags mark the paths. There is no fixed route; follow the tracks and turn back when you like.

Late afternoon is the best time. Farmers bring animals home, children come back from school, and the light turns warm on the terraces. Greet people with a namaste or tashi delek, and ask before photographing anyone or their house. Keep to the paths and do not walk across planted fields. Close any gate you open, and keep away from dogs guarding the farms. Watch where you step on narrow terrace edges.

The walk is free and easy, mostly on gentle slopes, though some tracks are steep and muddy after rain. Wear shoes with grip and carry a light jacket, because it cools quickly after 4 pm. If your hosts have time, ask one of them to come along. They will name the plants, tell you who lives where and show you short cuts back for tea. Do not pick fruit or flowers without asking.

faqs.q: What is there to do in Okhrey apart from Barsey
faqs.a: Okhrey is a quiet village, so the extras are simple: walk the farm lanes and terraces, visit the small village monastery, spend an evening in a Sherpa kitchen and watch the sunset from the road above. Rinchenpong and Uttarey are within a few hours if you want more.

faqs.q: Is Okhrey safe to walk around alone
faqs.a: Yes, Okhrey is a small, friendly village and generally safe to walk around alone in daylight. Keep to known tracks, tell your hosts where you are going, carry a torch if you might be out after dark, and give farm dogs a wide berth.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for walks around Okhrey
faqs.a: Not for village walks. The tracks are short and easy to follow, and you can always ask the way. A guide or your host adds stories and local names for plants and places. For longer forest walks or the ridge towards Barsey and beyond, a local guide is a good idea.

faqs.q: Where is Okhrey in Sikkim
faqs.a: Okhrey is a village at about 2,200 m in the far south-west of Sikkim, about 10 km above Sombaria and roughly 30 minutes by road below Hilley, the entry point for Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary. It is about 130 km from Siliguri, 5–6 hours via Jorethang, and close to the Nepal and West Bengal borders.

faqs.q: How do I reach Okhrey from Siliguri or NJP
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Jorethang, then a local jeep to Sombaria or Okhrey, about ₹150–250 a seat for the second leg, indicative, 2026. Leave early, as jeeps from Jorethang thin out after about 1 pm. A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹5,500–7,500 one way.

faqs.q: Is Okhrey or Hilley better for Barsey
faqs.a: Okhrey has more homestays and warmer, lower nights, and Hilley is only 30 minutes away by car. Hilley is right at the trail head but has little accommodation. For most travellers, sleeping in Okhrey and driving up at dawn is the better and cheaper choice.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Okhrey
faqs.a: March to May is best for rhododendrons, with peak bloom near Barsey usually mid-March to April. October to December brings clear skies and snow-peak views but no flowers. January and February are cold, with snow possible higher up. Avoid June to September, when rain and landslides slow the roads.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Okhrey and Barsey
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit for Okhrey but should carry photo ID; Barsey sanctuary charges an entry fee at Hilley. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available online or at the Melli checkpost, and pay a higher sanctuary fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How cold is Okhrey
faqs.a: At about 2,200 m, Okhrey is cold at night for most of the year. In March and April nights can drop close to freezing, and December to February brings frost and possible snow on the ridges above. Pack thermals, a warm jacket, a cap and socks, and expect quilts rather than heaters.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and shops in Okhrey
faqs.a: There is no ATM in Okhrey that we know of, and shops sell only basic snacks and household items. Withdraw cash in Siliguri or Jorethang before you come. UPI works when the network is good, but carry enough cash for your homestay, the car to Hilley and the sanctuary fee.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Okhrey and Barsey
faqs.a: Two nights is ideal: arrive on day one, walk to Barsey and back on day two, and leave on day three. One night works if you arrive early and walk the next morning. Add a night at Guras Kunj inside the sanctuary if you want sunrise from the ridge.

faqs.q: Can I combine Okhrey with Darjeeling
faqs.a: Yes. Darjeeling to Jorethang is about 30 km and 1.5–2 hours, and Jorethang to Okhrey about 2 hours more, so the two pair easily. A common plan is two nights in Darjeeling, two in Okhrey for Barsey, then on to Rinchenpong or Pelling. Check road conditions in the monsoon.
